2.text: and watched in all the weaker parts by old women and children. The herds-

3.text: men bring the herd, and first of all try to catch with their lassos, or by means

4.text: of the urine-tube, about ten harness-reindeer, which are placed at the entrance

5.text: of the corral; otherwise no free reindeer could be induced to enter it. Then

6.text: they drive the herd to and fro before the corral, picking out one by one

7.text: other harness-animals and driving them into the corral. The wildest ones are

8.text: caught with the lasso, which is thrown over them, or spread like a snare on

9.text: their track. When all the harness-reindeer are inside, the entrance is barred

10.text: with a heavy rope, and all the men and women immediately enter and secure

11.text: the reindeer with halters and traces. A few usually escape, breaking through

12.text: the corral, or jumping it; and sometimes the whole pack succeed in over-

13.text: throwing the sledges, and running away to join the herd. This happens

14.text: especially when any of the unbroken breeding-bucks have entered the corral

15.text: among the harness-reindeer. When all the animals are in their places, somebody

16.text: gives the signal, and all the sledges drop to position at the same moment

17.text: and start on, going in their respective lines. This difficult process requires

18.text: the help of several people, and occupies usually three or four hours. A small

19.text: family, living by chance in a separate camp, especially when lacking young,

20.text: swift men, will sometimes fail to catch their own harness-animals for two or

21.text: three days in succession. The Koryak and the Lamut harness-reindeer, on

22.text: the other hand, are taken without any corral, by means of a long leather

23.text: rope, which is drawn around the required animals (Plate VI, Fig. 2). All

24.text: those not surrounded by the rope will come in of their own will. Many can

25.text: be taken by hand. The whole operation takes not more than an hour.

26.text: Lieut. Polander,¹ as an eye-witness, describes one very docile Chukchee herd,

27.text: about fifty head strong, that every morning came to greet their master. Then,

28.text: at a signal of the master, the animals, which all the time stood in regular

29.text: line, wheeled about and walked away to the pasture in the same unbroken

30.text: order. I do not know the reason for this unusual docility. Possibly, since it

31.text: happened early in the morning, the animals were attracted by the pieces of

32.text: the large snow-clod, soaked with urine, that is carried out of the Chukchee

33.text: tent every morning and eagerly consumed by the reindeer when near at hand.

34.text: I can hardly imagine Chukchee reindeer, however, making turns at a given

35.text: signal, “like the crew on a man-of-war,” to use the words of Polander.

36.text: When driving a single sledge and stopping for the night in the open air,

37.text: the Chukchee traveller cannot turn his reindeer loose, because they would

38.text: probably go back to the herd, even if at a distance of forty or fifty miles,

39.text: or because he would not be able to catch them in the morning. The reindeer

40.text: are hobbled by means of a short noose tied loosely to one of the fore-feet of

41.text: the animal, so that it keeps continually treading on it with the hind-feet.
